import { Code2, Database, Shield, Workflow } from 'lucide-react';

An **endpoint** is a REST API route you build from blocks instead of code. You
give it a **method** and a **path**, then wire a graph: a request enters at a
**handler** node, flows through **data** and **logic** nodes, and terminates at a
**response** node that produces the HTTP response. It is the visual sibling of
[Functions](/build/functions). Where a function runs your code in a container,
an endpoint runs a graph **synchronously inside the API process**, so there is no
container and no cold start.

The graph is stored in the same shape as a [workflow](/automate/workflows) and
runs on the same hardened node executor. The difference is the contract:
Workflows are event- and schedule-driven and run asynchronously; an endpoint is
a synchronous request → response, which is why it lives in **Build** beside
Functions rather than in Automate.

<Callout title="Managing endpoints is a server task">
  Creating, updating and publishing endpoints changes your project's API
  surface, so do it from a trusted context with your project **API key**
  (`x-applad-key: <apiKey>`) or from the console, not from end-user code.
  *Calling* a published endpoint is a normal request whose auth the endpoint
  itself declares.
</Callout>

## The model: request, graph, response

An endpoint is a `method` + `path` + a graph of `nodes` and `edges`. Every node
can read a shared **request context**, and each node writes a named output that
later nodes reference by expression.

The request context is available to every node as `request`:

| Field | Contains |
| --- | --- |
| `request.method` | the HTTP method |
| `request.path` | the matched path |
| `request.params` | path parameters captured from the route (`/users/{id}` → `params.id`) |
| `request.query` | parsed query string |
| `request.headers` | request headers |
| `request.body` | the parsed JSON body |
| `request.user` | the caller's user id, if a session authenticated |
| `request.project` | the project id |

Nodes reference values with Go template expressions, either from the request or
from an earlier node's output by its **node id**:

```
{{.request.body.email}}      # a field from the request body
{{.createUser.$id}}          # the id of a row a "createUser" data node made
```

## Nodes

An endpoint reuses the whole [workflow node palette](/automate/workflows) for
logic and integrations, and adds three of its own.

### Handler

One `endpoint_handler` node marks the entry point. It carries no configuration
beyond the endpoint's method, path and auth (declared on the endpoint itself).

### Response

An `endpoint_response` node produces the HTTP response and ends the run. The
first response node reached wins, so branches can each end in their own response.

| Config | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `status` | HTTP status code (default `200`) |
| `mode` | `json` (default), `text`, `html`, or `error` |
| `bodyField` | a node id / dot path whose value becomes the body (e.g. `createUser`) |
| `body` | a template string; in `json` mode it is parsed as JSON when it is valid JSON |

### Data

An `endpoint_data` node reads or writes your [database](/build/databases). It is
the same row API a client SDK uses, so it is subject to the same
[permissions and row security](/build/permissions).

| Config | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `action` | `create`, `get`, `list` (or `query`), `update`, `delete` |
| `databaseId`, `tableId` | which table to act on (templatable) |
| `rowId` | the row for `get` / `update` / `delete` (templatable) |
| `data` | fields for `create` / `update`; string values are templated |
| `filters` | for `list`: `[{ "field": "status", "method": "equal", "value": "active" }]` |
| `limit`, `offset` | for `list` (default limit `25`) |
| `applyRules` | **the permission toggle** (see below), default `true` |

## The permission model

There are two independent layers, and keeping them distinct is the point.

**(a) Who may call the endpoint**, declared on the endpoint as `auth`:

| `auth` | Who may call |
| --- | --- |
| `public` | anyone |
| `session` | a request carrying a valid user session |
| `api_key` | a request carrying a project API key |
| `either` | a session **or** an API key |

**(b) What the nodes may touch**, the per-data-node `applyRules` toggle, which
chooses the database role the operation runs under:

<Callout title="Apply rules: scoped by default, elevated by choice">
  - **`applyRules: true`** (the default) runs the operation under the **caller's**
    role. Table grants and row security are enforced exactly as they are for a
    client SDK call. A public endpoint's caller is the anonymous role; an
    authenticated one carries the user's resolved roles and team memberships.
  - **`applyRules: false`** runs the operation under the elevated **service**
    role (full access) for admin operations the endpoint author deliberately
    trusts.
</Callout>

Because the two layers are separate, a **public** endpoint can still safely write
data: its nodes run as the anonymous role unless the author explicitly elevates a
node. Elevation is a visible choice, not a default.

## Calling an endpoint

A published endpoint is served under your project at `/v1/e/{path}`. Path
parameters in the template are captured into `request.params`.

```bash
curl -X POST https://api.applad.io/v1/e/signup \
  -H "x-applad-project: <projectId>" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"email":"ada@example.com","name":"Ada"}'
```

The router matches by method and path. A literal route (`/users/me`) beats a
parameterised one (`/users/{id}`) when both match. Only endpoints with status
`published` are served; a `draft` is reachable only from the console test runner.

## A worked example: a signup endpoint

`POST /signup` that creates a row and returns it. The `createUser` node runs with
`applyRules: false` because signup writes for a not-yet-authenticated caller, and
the response returns the new row.

```json
{
  "method": "POST",
  "path": "/signup",
  "auth": "public",
  "status": "published",
  "nodes": [
    { "id": "in",  "type": "endpoint_handler" },
    { "id": "createUser", "type": "endpoint_data", "config": {
        "action": "create", "databaseId": "app", "tableId": "users",
        "applyRules": false,
        "data": { "email": "{{.request.body.email}}", "name": "{{.request.body.name}}" }
    }},
    { "id": "out", "type": "endpoint_response", "config": {
        "status": 201, "bodyField": "createUser"
    }}
  ],
  "edges": [
    { "source": "in", "target": "createUser" },
    { "source": "createUser", "target": "out" }
  ]
}
```

Branch on a value with an `if_condition` node (from the workflow palette) and
give each branch its own response:

```json
{ "id": "check", "type": "if_condition", "config": {
    "field": "request.body.email", "operator": "not_empty",
    "trueBranch": "createUser", "falseBranch": "reject" }}
```

## Execution and performance

An endpoint runs **synchronously in the API process**: the request goroutine
executes the graph and returns. Because Go serves each request on its own
goroutine, a slow endpoint blocks only its own request, never the server. What
keeps it fast and safe on the shared API:

- **No cold start.** Inline dispatch is sub-millisecond; the latency is your
  database round-trips, not the executor.
- **A per-request deadline.** Each run is bounded (default 15s, override with
  `ENDPOINT_EXECUTION_TIMEOUT`); a run that exceeds it returns `504`.
- **A node cap.** A single endpoint graph is capped at 200 nodes.
- **Guarded egress.** Any node that calls outward goes through the same SSRF
  guard as workflows, so an endpoint cannot be turned into a pivot into internal
  services.

For genuinely heavy or long work, a node should hand off (call a
[Function](/build/functions) or enqueue a job) rather than doing it inline.

## Testing and history

While building, run an endpoint against a sample request without publishing it:

```bash
curl -X POST https://api.applad.io/v1/endpoints/<endpointId>/test \
  -H "x-applad-project: <projectId>" -H "x-applad-key: <apiKey>" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"body":{"email":"ada@example.com"}}'
```

The response includes the status, body, and a per-node **trace** so you can see
what each node produced. Every real call is recorded too; read recent runs with
`GET /v1/endpoints/<endpointId>/executions`.
